headline: Magnetic Bacteria Give Worms 43% Longer Lives
meta_description: Chinese researchers found that magnetotactic bacteria extend healthy lifespan in worms by 43% by suppressing a harmful form of cell death.
summary_short: Scientists at China's Hefei Institutes discovered that magnetic bacteria can dramatically extend lifespan while protecting brain and gut health in worms.
body:
In a finding that could reshape how scientists approach aging, researchers at the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science have demonstrated that a microscopic magnetic bacterium can extend the healthy lifespan of laboratory worms by over 43 percent. The team, led by Prof. An Xu, used Magnetospirillum magneticum AMB-1—a naturally occurring magnetotactic bacterium—to treat Caenorhabditis elegans, a standard model organism in aging research. Beyond the dramatic lifespan increase, the treated worms retained better neurological function and intestinal integrity as they aged. The breakthrough appears in Free Radical Biology and Medicine.

The real story lies not just in the numbers, but in how the bacteria work. Researchers discovered that AMB-1's magnetic structures, called magnetosomes, play the crucial role. Bacteria without functioning magnetosomes produced no longevity benefit—a finding that pinpointed exactly what matters. The mechanism involves blocking ferroptosis, a destructive form of cell death triggered by iron accumulation and oxidative damage. By reducing iron buildup and lipid peroxidation in worm cells, the bacteria essentially switched off an aging pathway. Several key genes including ftn-1, bli-3, and ads-1 were involved in this protective effect.

What makes this work especially promising is that it opens an entirely new frontier. While scientists have long pursued anti-aging drugs and genetic therapies, their safety profiles and real-world applicability remain uncertain. Magnetotactic bacteria offer something different: they already show strong biocompatibility with living organisms and have proven useful in drug delivery and cancer research. The Hefei team's findings suggest these microscopic magnets might extend healthy lifespan too—establishing what researchers call "a novel microbial strategy for anti-aging intervention" with potential applications in geriatric medicine. For an aging world searching for safe, practical solutions, that distinction matters.
quick_facts: Magnetotactic bacterium extended worm lifespan by 43.39 percent
Research led by Prof. An Xu at Hefei Institutes, China
Bacteria blocked ferroptosis, a harmful iron-linked form of cell death
Treated worms preserved neurological and intestinal health in old age
Published September 2026 in Free Radical Biology and Medicine
